source_text: Καὶ λευκότερον λοιπὸν καὶ συντόμως ἔγραψαν ὁμοούσιον τῷ Πατρὶ τὸν Υἱόν· τὰ γὰρ προειρημένα πάντα ταύτην ἔχει τὴν σημασίαν. Καὶ ὁ γογγυσμὸς αὐτῶν, ὅτι ἄγραφοί εἰσιν αἱ λέξεις, ἐλέγχεται παρ' αὐτῶν μάταιος, ἐξ ἀγράφων ἀσεβήσαντες· ἄγραφα δὲ τὸ, Ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, καὶ τὸ, Ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν· αἰτιῶνται, ὅτι ἐξ ἀγράφων μετ' εὐσεβείας νοουμένων λέξεων κατεκρίθησαν. Αὐτοὶ μὲν ὡς ἐκ κοπρίας ὄντες, ἐλάλησαν ἀληθῶς ἀπὸ γῆς· οἱ δὲ ἐπίσκοποι, οὐχ ἑαυτοῖς εὑρόντες τὰς λέξεις, ἀλλ' ἐκ Πατέρων ἔχοντες τὴν μαρτυρίαν, οὕτως ἔγρα ψαν. Ἐπίσκοποι γὰρ ἀρχαῖοι πρὸ ἐτῶν ἐγγύς που ἑκατὸν τριάκοντα τῆς μεγάλης Ῥώμης καὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας πόλεως γράφοντες ᾐτιάσαντο τοὺς ποίημα λέγοντας τὸν Υἱὸν καὶ μὴ ὁμοούσιον τῷ Πατρί· καὶ τοῦτο ἐγίνωσκεν Εὐσέβιος ὁ γενόμενος ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Καισαρείας, πρότερον μὲν συντρέχων τῇ Ἀρειανῇ αἱρέσει, ὕστερον δὲ ὑπογράψας ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἐν Νικαίᾳ συνόδῳ, ἔγραψε τοῖς ἰδίοις διαβεβαιούμενος, ὅτι καὶ τῶν παλαιῶν τινας λογίους καὶ ἐπιφανεῖς ἐπισκόπους καὶ συγγραφέας, ἔγνωμεν ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ θεότητος τῷ τοῦ ὁμοουσίου χρησαμένους ὀνόματι. Τί οὖν ἔτι τὴν Ἀρίμηνον ὀνομάζουσιν, ἐν ᾗ καθῃρέθησαν; Τί παραιτοῦνται τὴν ἐν Νικαίᾳ σύνοδον, ἐν ᾗ καὶ οἱ Πατέρες αὐτῶν ὑπέγραψαν, καὶ ὡμολόγησαν ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας καὶ ὁμοούσιον εἶναι τὸν Υἱὸν τῷ Πατρί; τί περιτρέχουσιν; οὐ γὰρ πρὸς μό νους τοὺς ἐν Νικαίᾳ ἐπισκόπους συνελθόντας, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἑαυτῶν μεγάλους ἐπισκόπους, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἰδίους λοιπὸν μάχονται. Τίνων οὖν εἰσι κληρονόμοι καὶ διάδοχοι; πῶς δύνανται λέγειν Πα τέρας τούτους, ὧν οὐκ ἀποδέχονται τὴν ὁμολογίαν τὴν καλῶς καὶ ἀποστολικῶς γραφεῖσαν; Ἐπεὶ, εἰ νομίζουσιν ἀντιλέγειν δύνασθαι, εἰπάτωσαν, μᾶλλον δὲ ἀποκρινάσθωσαν, ἵνα καὶ ἑαυτοῖς περιπίπτοντες ἐλεγχθῶσιν, εἰ πιστεύουσι λέγοντι τῷ Υἱῷ· Ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν· καὶ, Ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν Πατέρα; Ναὶ, εἴποιεν ἂν, ἐπειδὴ γέγραπται, πιστεύομεν. Ἀλλὰ καὶ Πῶς ἕν εἰσι, καὶ πῶς ὁ ἑωρακὼς τὸν Υἱὸν ἑώρακε καὶ τὸν Πατέρα, ἐὰν ἐρωτηθῶσιν εἰπεῖν, πάντως που φήσουσι, Δι' ὁμοιότητα· εἰ μὴ τέλεον συμπεπτώκασι τοῖς ἀδελφὰ φρονοῦσιν αὐτοῖς, καὶ λεγομένοις Ἀνομοίοις. Ἀλλ' ἐὰν πάλιν ἐρωτηθῶσι, Πῶς ὅμοιος; ἀποθρασυνόμενοι φήσουσιν· Ἀρετῇ τελείᾳ καὶ συμφωνίᾳ τὸ αὐτὸ θέλειν τῷ Πατρὶ, καὶ μὴ θέλειν ὅπερ ὁ Πατὴρ οὐ θέλει. Ἀλλὰ μαθέτωσαν, ὅτι ἐξ ἀρετῆς καὶ τοῦ θέλειν ὁμοιούμενος τῷ Θεῷ, ἔχει μὲν καὶ τοῦ τρέπεσθαι τὴν προαίρεσιν· οὐκ ἔστι δὲ οὕτως ὁ Λόγος, εἰ μὴ ἄρα ἐκ μέρους καὶ καθ' ἡμᾶς ὅμοιος, ὅτι μὴ καὶ κατ' οὐ σίαν ὅμοιός ἐστι. Ταῦτα δὲ ἴδια ἡμῶν τῶν γενητῶν καὶ κτιστὴν ἐχόντων τὴν φύσιν. Καὶ γὰρ καὶ ἡμεῖς, καίτοι μὴ δυνάμενοι ὅμοιοι κατ' οὐσίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ γενέ σθαι, ὅμως, ἐξ ἀρετῆς βελτιούμενοι, μιμούμεθα τὸν Θεὸν, χαρισαμένου καὶ τοῦτο τοῦ Κυρίου, καὶ λέγοντος· Γίνεσθε οἰκτίρμονες, ὡς ὁ Πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐστί. Γίνεσθε τέλειοι, ὡς ὁ Πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τέλειός ἐστι. Τρεπτὰ δὲ τὰ γενητὰ, οὐκ ἄν τις ἀρνήσαιτο, ἀγγέλων μὲν παραβάντων, τοῦ δὲ Ἀδὰμ παρακούσαντος, καὶ πάντων δεομένων τῆς τοῦ Λόγου χάριτος.
thought_title: The Fathers' terms are ancient and scriptural; the Arians' slogans are the real unwritten innovations
orientation: Athanasius is defending the Nicene term 'consubstantial' against the Arian objection that it is not a scriptural word, and is about to show that the Arians' own slogans are the true unwritten innovations.
pass_a_gloss: And more clearly henceforth and concisely they wrote the Son consubstantial with the Father; for all the things said before have this meaning. And their murmuring, that the words are unwritten, is refuted by them as vain, since they acted impiously from unwritten things; and unwritten are the 'from nothing' and the 'there was when he was not'; they accuse, because from unwritten words understood with piety they were condemned. They themselves, as being from dung, truly spoke from the earth; but the bishops, not finding the words for themselves, but having the testimony from the Fathers, wrote thus. For ancient bishops, about one hundred thirty years before, of great Rome and of our city, writing, accused those saying the Son a thing made and not consubstantial with the Father; and Eusebius, who became bishop of Caesarea, formerly running with the Arian heresy, but later signing in the very council in Nicaea, knew this, and wrote to his own people affirming, that also some of the ancients, learned and distinguished bishops and writers, we knew using the name of the consubstantial for the divinity of the Father and the Son. Why then do they still name Ariminum, in which they were deposed? Why do they reject the council in Nicaea, in which also their fathers signed, and confessed the Son to be from the substance and consubstantial with the Father? Why do they run about? For not only against the bishops who came together in Nicaea, but also against their own great bishops, and against their own henceforth they fight. Of whom then are they heirs and successors? How can they call fathers these, whose confession, written well and apostolically, they do not accept? Since, if they think they can contradict, let them say, or rather let them answer, so that also falling upon themselves they may be refuted, whether they believe the Son saying: 'I and the Father are one'; and, 'The one who has seen me has seen the Father'? Yes, they would say, since it is written, we believe. But also how they are one, and how the one who has seen the Son has seen also the Father, if they are asked to say, certainly they will say, 'Through likeness'; unless they have completely fallen in with those who think the same as them, and are called Anomoeans. But if again they are asked, 'How is he like?', becoming bold they will say: 'By perfect virtue and harmony, to will the same as the Father, and not to will what the Father does not will.' But let them learn, that the one being made like God from virtue and from willing has also the choice of turning; but the Word is not thus, unless indeed he is like in part and according to us, because he is not also like according to substance. But these things are proper to us, the created things, who have a created nature. For also we, although not able to become like God according to substance, nevertheless, being improved from virtue, imitate God, the Lord also granting this, and saying: 'Become merciful, as your Father is merciful.' 'Become perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.' But that created things are changeable, no one would deny, since angels transgressed, and Adam disobeyed, and all need the grace of the Word.

pass_b_english: And so at last they wrote more clearly and concisely that the Son is consubstantial with the Father; for all that had been said before carries this meaning. And their grumbling that these words are unwritten is shown by their own conduct to be empty, since they committed impiety from unwritten words. For 'from nothing' and 'there was when he was not' are unwritten, yet they complain that they were condemned from unwritten words understood with reverence. They, as being from dung, truly spoke from the earth; but the bishops did not invent the words for themselves—they had the testimony from the Fathers, and so they wrote. For ancient bishops of great Rome and of our own city, writing nearly one hundred and thirty years before, censured those who said the Son was a thing made and not consubstantial with the Father. And Eusebius, who became bishop of Caesarea, knew this: formerly he sided with the Arian heresy, but later he signed at the council in Nicaea itself, and he wrote to his own people affirming that we know that some of the ancient learned and distinguished bishops and writers used the term 'consubstantial' for the divinity of the Father and the Son.

Why then do they still name Ariminum, where they were deposed? Why do they reject the council in Nicaea, where their own Fathers signed and confessed that the Son is from the substance and consubstantial with the Father? Why do they run about? For they are fighting not only against the bishops who gathered at Nicaea, but also against their own great bishops, and against their own people at last. Whose heirs and successors are they then? How can they call those men Fathers whose confession, written so well and in apostolic fashion, they do not accept? For if they think they can contradict it, let them speak—or rather, let them answer, so that they may be caught in their own trap and exposed—whether they believe the Son when he says, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and, 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). Yes, they might say, since it is written, we believe.

But if they are asked to say how they are one, and how the one who has seen the Son has also seen the Father, they will surely say, 'Through likeness'—unless they have completely collapsed into the company of those who think like them and are called Anomoeans. But if they are asked again, 'How is he like?' they will boldly say, 'By perfect virtue and harmony, in willing the same as the Father and not willing what the Father does not will.' But let them learn that one who is made like God by virtue and by willing has a choice that can also turn and change. The Word is not like that—unless he is like us only in part and in our manner, because he is not like according to substance. These things belong to us, created things whose nature is created. For we too, although we cannot become like God in substance, nevertheless, as we improve in virtue, we imitate God, since the Lord grants this and says, 'Be merciful, as your Father is merciful' (Luke 6:36), and 'Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect' (Matthew 5:48). But no one would deny that created things are changeable: angels transgressed, Adam disobeyed, and all things need the grace of the Word.

last_rejected.quote: since they committed impiety from unwritten words
last_rejected.why: Misreads participle: Arians are condemned FOR impiety from unwritten words, not 'committed impiety from' them.
last_rejected.fix: since they were condemned for impiety on the basis of unwritten words
last_rejected.ruling: ἀσεβήσαντες is aorist participle: 'having committed impiety from unwritten words'—English 'since they committed' correctly renders causal participle.

last_rejected.quote: yet they complain that they were condemned from unwritten words understood with reverence
last_rejected.source_quote: αἰτιῶνται, ὅτι ἐξ ἀγράφων μετ' εὐσεβείας νοουμένων λέξεων κατεκρίθησαν
last_rejected.why: Wrong subject: the bishops (not Arians) were condemned; Arians 'complain/accuse' this was unjust.
last_rejected.fix: yet they complain that the bishops were condemned by unwritten words understood piously
last_rejected.ruling: κατεκρίθησαν passive: 'they were condemned' refers to Arians; αἰτιῶνται 'they complain'—English correctly captures Arians complaining about their own condemnation.

last_rejected.quote: They, as being from dung, truly spoke from the earth
last_rejected.source_quote: Αὐτοὶ μὲν ὡς ἐκ κοπρίας ὄντες, ἐλάλησαν ἀληθῶς ἀπὸ γῆς
last_rejected.why: ἀληθῶς goes with 'from the earth' (truly earthly), not 'truly spoke'; 'truly' misplaced changes sense.
last_rejected.fix: They, as being from dung, spoke truly from the earth
last_rejected.ruling: ἀληθῶς ἀπὸ γῆς ἐλάλησαν: 'truly spoke from the earth' is valid; ἀληθῶς can modify the verb, not necessarily 'earthly'.

last_rejected.quote: we know that some of the ancient learned and distinguished bishops and writers used
last_rejected.source_quote: ἔγνωμεν ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ θεότητος τῷ τοῦ ὁμοουσίου χρησαμένους ὀνόματι
last_rejected.why: ἔγνωμεν is 'we knew/learned' (Eusebius's claim), not 'we know'; present tense misrepresents his letter.
last_rejected.fix: we learned that some of the ancient learned and distinguished bishops and writers had used
last_rejected.ruling: ἔγνωμεν can mean 'we know' or 'we knew'; present perfect sense is within normal range; not a clear error.

last_rejected.quote: against their own people at last
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἰδίους λοιπὸν μάχονται
last_rejected.why: τοὺς ἰδίους refers to 'their own [Fathers/bishops]', not 'their own people'; 'people' changes meaning.
last_rejected.fix: and against their own as well at last
last_rejected.ruling: τοὺς ἰδίους 'their own' is general; 'people' is a reasonable rendering, not clearly wrong.

last_rejected.quote: unless they have completely collapsed into the company of those who think like them and are called Anomoeans
last_rejected.source_quote: εἰ μὴ τέλεον συμπεπτώκασι τοῖς ἀδελφὰ φρονοῦσιν αὐτοῖς, καὶ λεγομένοις Ἀνομοίοις
last_rejected.why: ἀδελφὰ φρονοῦσιν αὐτοῖς means 'those thinking the same things as them' (allies), not 'like them' ambiguously.
last_rejected.fix: unless they have completely collapsed into the company of those who think the same as them and are called Anomoeans
last_rejected.ruling: ἀδελφὰ φρονοῦσιν αὐτοῖς: 'think like them' adequately renders 'thinking the same as them'; minor ambiguity, not major error.

last_rejected.quote: because he is not like according to substance
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅτι μὴ καὶ κατ' οὐσίαν ὅμοιός ἐστι
last_rejected.why: ὅτι μὴ = 'since he is not' (causal), not 'because'; and 'like' needs object: like the Father.
last_rejected.fix: since he is not like the Father according to substance
last_rejected.ruling: ὅτι μὴ here means 'except/unless' continuing the conditional; 'because' is awkward but context 'unless…because not' is intelligible; not clearly major.

last_rejected.quote: as we improve in virtue, we imitate God
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐξ ἀρετῆς βελτιούμενοι, μιμούμεθα τὸν Θεόν
last_rejected.why: βελτιούμενοι is passive/middle 'being improved/made better', not active 'as we improve'; agency shifted.
last_rejected.fix: as we are improved in virtue, we imitate God
last_rejected.ruling: βελτιούμενοι middle/passive 'being improved' can mean 'improving'; 'as we improve' is within normal range of meaning.
